claim: Catecholamines modulate the impact of motivational cues on action.
source: Catecholamines modulate the impact of motivational cues on action.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract introducing the research topic.

claim: Motivational biases have been proposed to reflect cue-based, 'Pavlovian' effects.
source: Such motivational biases have been proposed to reflect cue-based, 'Pavlovian' effects.
evidence: This statement references existing theoretical proposals in the literature.

claim: Motivational biases reflect both Pavlovian and instrumental effects: reward and punishment cues promoted generalized (in)action in a Pavlovian manner, whereas outcomes enhanced instrumental (un)learning of chosen actions.
source: Computational analyses showed that motivational biases reflect both Pavlovian and instrumental effects: reward and punishment cues promoted generalized (in)action in a Pavlovian manner, whereas outcomes enhanced instrumental (un)learning of chosen actions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from computational analyses presented in the study.

claim: Cue- and outcome-based biases were altered independently by the catecholamine enhancer methylphenidate.
source: These cue- and outcome-based biases were altered independently by the catecholamine enhancer melthylphenidate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation experiment.

claim: Methylphenidate's effect varied across individuals with a putative proxy of baseline dopamine synthesis capacity, working memory span.
source: Methylphenidate's effect varied across individuals with a putative proxy of baseline dopamine synthesis capacity, working memory span.
evidence: This is a primary finding showing individual differences in drug effects.

claim: Deficits in learning, action, and motivation are observed in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, Parkinson's disease, and addiction.
source: Deficits in these aspects of adaptive behaviour are observed in a wide range of neuropsychiatric disorders, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, Parkinson's disease, and addiction (Dagher and Robbins, 2009; Prince, 2008; Skolnick, 2005)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Many deficits in neuropsychiatric disorders can be treated with catecholaminergic drugs.
source: and many of those deficits can be treated with catecholaminergic drugs (Faraone and Buitelaar, 2010; Wigal et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Dopamine has been linked to behavioural activation in the context of reward.
source: The neuromodulator dopamine has been linked particularly strongly to behavioural activation in the context of reward (Taylor and Robbins, 1986; 1984)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dopamine amplifies the perceived benefits of action over their costs.
source: putatively by amplifying the perceived benefits of action over their costs (Collins and Frank, 2014; Niv et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a theoretical mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Appetitive cues elicit innately specified responses that may potentiate instrumental responding.
source: In PIT, conditioned cues elicit innately specified responses that may potentiate (or interfere with) instrumental responding, e.g. appetitive cues promote active responding (appetitive PIT), whereas aversive cues increase behavioural inhibition (aversive PIT; Davis and Wright, 1979; Huys et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the Pavlovian-instrumental transfer phenomenon with supporting citations.

claim: Enhanced dopamine increases appetitive PIT.
source: Enhanced dopamine increases appetitive PIT (Wyvell and Berridge, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Appetitive PIT is lowered when striatal dopamine is reduced.
source: while appetitive PIT is lowered when striatal dopamine is reduced (Dickinson et al., 2000; Hebart and Gläscher, 2015; Lex and Hauber, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Striatal dopamine has been linked to controlling aversively motivated behaviour.
source: Striatal dopamine has also been linked to controlling aversively motivated behaviour (Faure et al., 2008; Lloyd and Dayan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subjects successfully learned the task, as evidenced by increased Go responding to cues indicating the need to Go vs. NoGo.
source: Subjects successfully learned this difficult task, in which they needed to identify the correct response out of 3 options (Go-left/Go-right/NoGo) for eight different cues, as evidenced by increased Go responding to cues indicating the need to Go vs. NoGo (Required Action: X2(1)=624.3; p<0.001; Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is a behavioral result supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: Cue valence influenced Go responding, reflecting a motivational bias in responding.
source: As expected, cue valence also influenced Go responding (Valence: X2(1)=40.0; p<0.001), reflecting a motivational bias in responding.
evidence: This is a behavioral result supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Subjects made more Go responses for Win than Avoid cues.
source: Overall subjects made more Go responses for Win than Avoid cues.
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the data.

claim: The effect of cue valence was highly significant for both Go and NoGo cues.
source: The effect of cue valence was highly significant for both Go and NoGo cues (Go cues: X2(1)=37.5, p<0.001; NoGo cues: X2(1)=13.3, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: The motivational bias was present for both correct and incorrect Go responses.
source: Subjects made more Go responses to Win than avoid cues for both correct (Valence: X2(1)=26.1, p<0.001) and incorrect (Valence: X2(1)=25.6, p<0.001) Go responses.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data.

claim: Stepwise addition of the go bias, Pavlovian response bias and instrumental learning bias parameter improved model fit.
source: Stepwise addition of the go bias (Appendix 5), Pavlovian response bias and instrumental learning bias parameter improved model fit, as quantified by Watanabe-Akaike Information Criteria (WAIC; Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is a computational modeling result supported by model comparison metrics.

claim: The Pavlovian bias parameter estimates (π) of the winning model M4 were positive across the group (96.4% of posterior distribution >0).
source: The Pavlovian bias parameter estimates (π) of the winning model M4 were positive across the group (96.4% of posterior distribution >0).
evidence: This is a computational modeling result from Bayesian parameter estimation.

claim: The biased instrumental learning parameter estimates were positive across the group (100% of posterior distribution >0).
source: The biased instrumental learning parameter estimates were also positive across the group (100% of posterior distribution >0).
evidence: This is a computational modeling result from Bayesian parameter estimation.

claim: MPH enhanced the effect of cue valence on Go responding proportional to working memory span.
source: MPH enhanced the effect of cue valence on Go responding proportional to working memory span (Valence x Drug x Listening Span: X2(1)=5.9; p=0.016; Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation experiment.

claim: There was no Valence x Drug effect across the group.
source: in the absence of a Valence x Drug effect across the group (Valence x Drug: X2(1)=1.5; p=0.221; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no main effect of drug.

claim: High-span subjects showed a drug-induced increase in motivational bias, while low-span subjects showed a drug-induced decrease in motivational bias.
source: While high-span subjects showed a drug-induced increase in motivational bias (MPH versus placebo increased Go responding to Win vs. Avoid cues), low-span subjects showed a drug-induced decrease in motivational bias.
evidence: This describes the pattern of individual differences in drug effects.

claim: The span-dependent bias emerged under MPH and was not significant under placebo.
source: This span-dependent bias emerged under MPH (X2(1)=4.6, p=0.032), and was not significant under placebo (X2(1)=0.9, p=0.335; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing drug-specific effects.

claim: The MPH effect was driven by incorrect Go responses.
source: A break-down of this effect into correct and incorrect responses revealed that it was driven by incorrect Go responses (Valence x Drug x Listening Span: X2(1)=11.9, p<0.001; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral analysis.

claim: MPH did not significantly affect the correct Go responses.
source: MPH did not significantly affect the correct Go responses (Valence x Drug x Listening Span: X2(1)=2.0, p=0.152).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no effect on correct responses.

claim: Trait impulsivity did not significantly predict the effect of MPH on the motivational bias.
source: In contrast to listening span, trait impulsivity did not significantly predict the effect of MPH on the motivational bias (all p>0.05; see Appendix 3 for an overview of the mixed model effects).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no relationship with impulsivity.

claim: Model fit improved markedly when extending the winning base model M4 with the MPH-induced Pavlovian bias parameter πMPH (M5a).
source: Model fit improved markedly when extending the winning base model M4 with the MPH-induced Pavlovian bias parameter πMPH (M5a; Figure 5; Table 2).
evidence: This is a computational modeling result from model comparison.

claim: The MPH-induced diffuse learning bias parameter κMPH-diffuse (M5c) strongly improved model fit relative to base model M4.
source: Conversely, the MPH-induced diffuse learning bias parameter κMPH-diffuse (M5c) also strongly improved model fit relative to base model M4.
evidence: This is a computational modeling result from model comparison.

claim: The MPH modulation of Pavlovian bias and diffuse learning parameters both covaried with Listening Span.
source: Confirming the model comparison results, the MPH modulation of Pavlovian bias and diffuse learning parameters both covaried with Listening Span (πMPH: R = 0.25, p=0.013; κMPH-diffuse: R = 0.28, p=0.006)
evidence: This is a statistical result showing correlation with working memory span.

claim: The MPH selective learning bias did not covary with Listening Span.
source: while the MPH selective learning bias did not (κMPH-selective: R = −0.01, p=0.9).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no correlation.

claim: Model comparison showed that the composite model M6 containing both πMPH and κMPH-diffuse explained the data best.
source: Model comparison showed that indeed this composite model explained the data best (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a computational modeling result from model comparison.

claim: In model M6, both πMPH and κMPH-diffuse parameters significantly varied proportional to Listening Span.
source: In this model, both parameters again significantly varied proportional to Listening Span (πMPH: R = 0.24, p=0.020; κMPH-diffuse: R = 0.22, p=0.032; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the winning computational model.

claim: MPH alters the impact of cue valence on action, which is present and persists from the first trial onward.
source: In other words, MPH (i) alters the impact of cue valence on action, which is present and persists from the first trial onward
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results.

claim: MPH alters the impact of rewarding outcomes on the learning of actions, which fully depends on and evolves with experience.
source: and (ii) alters the impact of rewarding outcomes on the learning of actions, which fully depends on and evolves with experience.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the computational modeling results.

claim: Following a reward, the effect of κMPH-diffuse is to increase the value of incorrect Go responses in addition to the correct Go response.
source: Following a reward, the effect of κMPH-diffuse is to increase the value of incorrect Go responses in addition to the correct Go response.
evidence: This describes the computational mechanism of the diffuse learning parameter.

claim: Model M6 can capture the observed effects, replicating the Listening Span dependent effect of MPH on choice.
source: Both methods confirmed that M6 can capture the observed effects, replicating the Listening Span dependent effect of MPH on choice, where MPH increased Go responses to Win vs. Avoid cues more in higher span subjects (simulations: R = 0.27, p=0.008; one-step-ahead: R = 0.20, p=0.050; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a model validation result using simulation and prediction methods.

claim: Cue valence elicits behavioural activation in a Pavlovian manner, whereas outcome valence biases the learning of action vs. inhibition.
source: First, cue valence elicits behavioural activation in a Pavlovian manner, whereas outcome valence biases the learning of action vs. inhibition (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: MPH modulates Pavlovian biasing, while also altering the reward-driven diffusion of credit assignment during instrumental learning.
source: Second, MPH modulates Pavlovian biasing, while also altering the reward-driven diffusion of credit assignment during instrumental learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: The direction of the effect of MPH covaries with individual differences in working memory span, but not trait impulsivity.
source: Third, the direction of the effect of MPH covaries with individual differences in working memory span, but not trait impulsivity.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: Dopamine bursts elicited by reward prediction errors enhance long-term potentiation of the corticostriatal synapses associated with the just-performed response.
source: Here, dopamine bursts elicited by reward prediction errors (Montague et al., 2004; Schultz et al., 1998; Schultz et al., 1997) during the outcome, enhance long-term potentiation (LTP) of the corticostriatal synapses associated with the just-performed response (Frank et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a theoretical mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Prolonged release of dopamine after DAT blockade might reduce selectivity and diffuse the specificity of credit assignment.
source: Thus, prolonged release of DA (e.g. after DAT blockade) might reduce this selectivity, and diffuse the specificity of credit assignment.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on known mechanisms.

claim: Striatal dopamine dips following negative prediction errors can drive avoidance by promoting long-term depression in the 'Go' pathway and LTP in the 'NoGo' pathway.
source: Conversely, striatal dopamine dips following negative prediction errors can drive avoidance by promoting long-term depression (LTD) in the 'Go' pathway and LTP in the 'NoGo' pathway (Beeler et al., 2012; Frank, 2005; Shen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a theoretical mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Transient optogenetic inhibition of dopamine induces behavioural avoidance of recently selected actions.
source: Indeed, transient optogenetic inhibition of DA induces behavioural avoidance of recently selected actions (Danjo et al., 2014; Hamid et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: The avoidance effect of dopamine inhibition depends on D2 receptors.
source: an effect that depends on D2 receptors (Danjo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: D2 neurons are excited in response to losses.
source: D2 neurons are excited in response to losses (Zalocusky et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Activation of D2 neurons during losses induces subsequent avoidance learning.
source: their activation during losses induces subsequent avoidance learning (Kravitz et al., 2012; Zalocusky et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Disruption of D2 neurons prevents avoidance learning.
source: and their disruption prevents avoidance learning (Hikida et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claim: Blocking catecholamine reuptake with MPH altered the extent to which subjects were influenced by the cue and outcome valence.
source: Blocking the reuptake of catecholamines with MPH altered the extent to which subjects were influenced by the cue and outcome valence.
evidence: This is a summary of the pharmacological manipulation results.

claim: Blocking catecholamine reuptake with MPH extends the duration of dopamine presence in the synaptic cleft.
source: Blocking catecholamine reuptake with MPH extends the duration of dopamine presence in the synaptic cleft (Dreyer and Hounsgaard, 2013).
evidence: This is a known pharmacological mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Prolonged dopamine presence would be less selective in potentiating the actions that were selected immediately prior to rewards.
source: This prolonged dopamine presence (i.e. reduced temporal specificity) would be less selective in potentiating the actions that were selected immediately prior to rewards (e.g. Yagishita et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on known mechanisms and cited work.

claim: Individuals vary strongly in the extent to which MPH increases extracellular dopamine.
source: Individuals vary strongly in the extent to which MPH increases extracellular dopamine (Volkow et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Working memory span is related to dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: working memory span, given its known relation to dopamine synthesis capacity (Cools et al., 2008; Landau et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to PET studies.

claim: Trait impulsivity is related to D2 (auto)receptor availability.
source: trait impulsivity, for its known relation to D2 (auto)receptor availability (Buckholtz et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2009; Reeves et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Baseline dopamine cell activity is a better predictor of effects of MPH than either D2 auto-receptor availability or DAT occupancy under MPH.
source: Indeed, baseline dopamine cell activity is a better predictor of effects of MPH than either D2 auto-receptor availability or DAT occupancy under MPH (Volkow et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: MPH increased subjective experiences of positive affect and alertness, and decreased calmness.
source: Across subjects, MPH increased subjective experiences of positive affect and alertness, and decreased calmness (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from mood assessments.

claim: MPH-induced mood changes did not covary with working memory span.
source: In contrast to the MPH-induced Pavlovian response bias and diffuse learning bias, these non-specific mood changes did not covary with working memory span.
evidence: This is a statistical result showing no correlation.

claim: The MPH effect on Pavlovian activation and biased instrumental learning cannot be attributed to MPH-induced changes in mood.
source: Therefore, the MPH effect on Pavlovian activation and biased instrumental learning cannot be attributed to MPH-induced changes in mood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between mood and the effects of interest.

claim: MPH blocks the dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, thereby diminishing the reuptake of catecholamines.
source: MPH blocks the dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, thereby diminishing the reuptake of catecholamines.
evidence: This is a known pharmacological mechanism.

claim: When administered orally, MPH has a maximal plasma concentration after 2 hr and a plasma half-life of 2–3 hr.
source: When administered orally, MPH has a maximal plasma concentration after 2 hr and a plasma half-life of 2–3 hr (Kimko et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a pharmacokinetic property supported by citation.

claim: The motivational Go/NoGo learning task was performed on average 2 hr after capsule intake, well within the peak of plasma concentration.
source: On average the motivational Go/NoGo learning task was performed 2 hr after capsule intake, well within the peak of plasma concentration.
evidence: This describes the timing of the experimental procedure.

claim: The study collected a large sample of 106 native Dutch volunteers.
source: we collected a large sample of 106 native Dutch volunteers (aged 18–28 years, mean (SD) = 21.5 (2.3); 53 women; 84 right-handed; sample size calculation reported in CMO protocol NL47166.091.13).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: Four subjects dropped out after the first test day.
source: Four subjects dropped out after the first test day (due to too much delay between test days, loss of motivation, nausea, and mild arrhythmia).
evidence: This describes attrition in the study sample.

claim: Two subjects dissolved the capsules before swallowing and were discarded because of uncertainty in the pharmacodynamics.
source: Two subjects dissolved the capsules before swallowing and are discarded because of uncertainty in the pharmacodynamics.
evidence: This describes exclusion criteria applied during the study.

claim: One subject did not sufficiently engage in the task and was discarded.
source: One subject did not sufficiently engage in the task (only 13/2% Go responses on day 1/2) and was discarded as well.
evidence: This describes exclusion criteria applied during the study.

claim: Of the resulting 99 subjects, 48 subjects received MPH on the first day.
source: Of the resulting 99 subjects, 48 subjects received MPH on the first day.
evidence: This describes the final sample and counterbalancing.

claim: Feedback validity was 80%, that is, correct (incorrect) responses were followed by the desirable outcome 80% (20%) of the time.
source: Feedback validity was 80%, that is, correct (incorrect) responses were followed by the desirable outcome 80% (20%) of the time (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: Each cue was presented 40 times.
source: Each cue was presented 40 times.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: The task lasted approximately 30 min, including instructions and a self-paced break halfway.
source: The task lasted approximately 30 min, including instructions and a self-paced break halfway.
evidence: This describes the task duration.

claim: Working memory span was assessed with the Listening Span Test.
source: Working memory span was assessed with the Listening Span Test (Daneman and Carpenter, 1980; Salthouse and Babcock, 1991)
evidence: This describes the assessment method with citations.

claim: The Listening Span Test was used in two FMT PET studies showing positive correlations with striatal dopamine synthesis capacity.
source: which was also used in two FMT PET studies showing positive correlations with striatal dopamine synthesis capacity (Cools et al., 2008; Landau et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to PET studies.

claim: Trait impulsivity was assessed with the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11).
source: Trait impulsivity was assessed with the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11) (Patton et al., 1995).
evidence: This describes the assessment method with citation.

claim: The BIS-11 total impulsivity scores reflect the tendency towards impulsivity.
source: The BIS-11 total impulsivity scores reflect the tendency towards impulsivity.
evidence: This describes what the measure assesses.

claim: In all models, action weights are estimated for each response option for all trials per cue.
source: In all models, action weights (w) are estimated for each response option (a) for all trials (t) per cue (s).
evidence: This describes the computational modeling approach.

claim: WAIC is an estimate of the likelihood of the data given the model parameters, penalized for the effective number of parameters to adjust for overfitting.
source: WAIC is an estimate of the likelihood of the data given the model parameters, penalized for the effective number of parameters to adjust for overfitting.
evidence: This describes the model comparison metric.

claim: Lower (i.e. more negative) WAIC values indicate better model fit.
source: Lower (i.e. more negative) WAIC values indicate better model fit.
evidence: This describes how to interpret the model comparison metric.

claim: A difference in WAIC value of 2–6 is considered positive evidence, 6–10 strong evidence, and >10 very strong evidence.
source: As WAIC is reported on the deviance scale (Gelman et al., 2014), a difference in WAIC value of 2–6 is considered positive evidence, 6–10 strong evidence, and >10 very strong evidence (Kass and Raftery, 1995).
evidence: This describes the interpretation guidelines with citations.
